https://www.politico.eu/article/france-w.text: France’s wine production is expected to fall below 3.4 billion liters this year as drought and repeated heat waves battered vineyards across the country, with the Champagne region worst affected, according to French government estimates published Monday. The brutal summer weather pulled harvests dramatically forward. Most French vineyards began picking in August after exceptionally high temperatures accelerated ripening. “Soil drought intensified across the entire country,” the Agriculture Ministry's statistics service Agreste said, while heat waves caused “sunscald, burns, defoliation and grape shriveling” in some vineyards. Advertisement Advertisement In Champagne, growers reaped their earliest harvest on record, racing to pick grapes before rising sugar levels pushed potential alcohol too high. Output there is expected to be roughly halved , with grape bunch weights at their lowest in 20 years. In southern France’s Languedoc-Roussillon wine region, by contrast, production is forecast to rebound 5 percent from last year’s weak harvest, which was about 13 percent below the five-year average. Even with that recovery, output this year remains 8 percent below average. Conditions had initially looked promising, with good grape development and low disease pressure. But “the hot and dry conditions of the summer degraded this potential,” Agreste said. If confirmed, the sub-3.4 billion-liter crop would be France’s smallest since 1957 — a nearly 70-year low . And wine is only one casualty of Europe’s brutal summer. Farmer group Copa-Cogeca estimated in a report published last week that maize losses reached 50 to 70 percent in Slovenia, 40 percent in France and 20 to 25 percent in Italy, reaching 70 percent in some unirrigated areas. Croatia expects fruit and grape output to fall around 30 percent. French Environment Minister Monique Barbut has put the summer’s economic damage at €10 billion to €15 billion , or as much as 0.5 percent of GDP. Paris unveiled more than €1 billion in emergency farm aid Friday, though agricultural groups say the package falls short. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/entertainme.text: Seoul International Music Festival (SIMF) Orchestra / Courtesy of SIMF Ryu Jea-joon, artistic director of Seoul International Music Festival (SIMF), speaks during a press conference in Seoul, Sept. 16. Courtesy of SIMF The Seoul International Music Festival (SIMF) returns for its 18th edition with a curated series of classical music to offer comfort, hope and joy to audiences. The festival will present seven concerts from Oct. 8-16 at the Seoul Arts Center and Lotte Concert Hall in Seoul under the central theme "Bravo My Life!" Artistic Director Ryu Jea-joon framed the seven concerts into a single narrative arc reflecting human existence. The journey begins with the opening concert "Breath" and continues through "Three Portraits," "Serenade," "Light and Shadow," "Wonderful Memories," "Dichterliebe" and the closing concert "Humanity, That Brilliant Journey." "We prepared classical music with care to deliver comfort, hope and joy, encouraging everyone who lives their daily lives faithfully," Ryu said during a recent press conference. "I hope the beautiful music played by these precious artists offers small strength, courage and warm comfort to your lives." A poster for Seoul International Music Festival (SIMF) / Courtesy of SIMF He said the festival will bring together musicians carrying their own stories from countries around the world, including the Czech Republic, Spain, Austria, the United States, Hungary and Poland. "The music of harmony created by people with different backgrounds symbolizes the beauty of our society where diversity exists," Ryu said. "When we accept our differences and bless our own lives, we can become even brighter beings." Key performers include cellist Arto Noras, tenor Ian Bostridge, trumpeter Sergei Nakariakov, hornist Radovan Vlatkovic and violinist Elina Vahala. Polish conductor Krzysztof Urbanski, artistic director of the Warsaw Philharmonic Orchestra, will make his Korean debut leading the festival's closing concert on Oct. 16 at Lotte Concert Hall. He will conduct the SIMF Orchestra in a massive 103-piece configuration. The SIMF Orchestra serves as the festival's centerpiece alongside Ensemble Opus, featuring top Korean instrumentalists such as violinist Song Ji-won, violist Kim Sang-jin and hornist Kim Hong-bak. Emerging young talents including violinist Lee Hyun-jung and cellist Lee Jae-ri will also join the orchestra for the first time. This year's festival will also celebrate the 150th anniversary of Polish Romantic composer Mieczyslaw Karlowicz (1876-1909) by featuring his works for the Korean audiences as part of a cultural exchange program with Poland. Founded in 2009, the annual event has established itself as one of Korea's premier classical music festivals. Tickets are available through major venue platforms, with special ticket donation programs arranged for underprivileged groups. For details, visit the Seoul International Music Festival’s official website .

https://www.dw.com/en/zelenskyy-visits-n.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OU7m Zelenskyy hugged US envoy Steve Witkoff at the meeting with Finnish and Norwegian leaders looking on Image: Heiko Junge/NTB/AFP Advertisement Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited Norway on Tuesday as Ukraine faces renewed tension in its relationship with US President Donald Trump and his administration. Finland's Stubb: 'Today was a good day for peace' During the visit, Zelenskyy met with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, along with Trump envoy Steve Witkoff. The US president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, joined the meeting remotely. Store described the meeting involving the European and the US sides as "good and constructive" at a press conference. "US and European teams have done substantive work on key issues together with Ukraine," Store said. Stubb said, "Today was a good day for peace." The Finnish president said Witkoff intends to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders and discuss ideas from the Oslo meeting. Trump envoy Steve Witkoff was not present at the press conference after the meeting Image: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP The Oslo meeting comes as Zelenskyy has accused the US of withholding intelligence from Ukraine in advance of Russian strikes and delaying the delivery of interceptor missiles. Zelenskyy: Early intel warnings from partners on Russian strikes resume Zelenskyy said he held a phone call with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier in the day and said Ukraine is now receiving early warnings from its partners ahead of Russian strikes. "We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said of the Russian-launched missiles while standing next to Finnish and Norwegian leaders. There are also media reports that Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping could hold a meeting to possibly discuss Ukraine and other issues. "I don't know what the trilateral meeting will be about between America and China, and Russia, it's up to them," Zelenskyy said, but added that if Ukraine is discussed, it would be acceptable only if Ukrainians are at the negotiating table. Trump ramps up attacks on Zelenskyy as US midterms loom Earlier this month, Zelenskyy criticized a deal struck between the Trump administration and Russia to buy Russian diesel fuel . Oil and gas export revenues are vital for the Russian economy and war efforts in Ukraine . How Trump is helping Putin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Trump has criticized Zelenskyy and blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries for high diesel prices. Prices have increased dramatically since Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in response to US attacks. Zelenskyy on Tuesday said he is supportive of Trump's suggestion to stop attacks on energy sites, with Russia also doing the same in regard to Ukraine as part of an "energy ceasefire." However, Zelenskyy said Russia is unwilling to stop its attacks on Ukraine. At a recent European Union summit in Brussels , Zelenskyy smiled at the suggestion that he is being made a scapegoat by Trump. The US president is looking for someone else to blame for high domestic energy costs ahead of midterm congressional elections onb November 3. If the opposition Democrats take back control of the US House and Senate, it could constrain Trump's powers in his last two years in office. In comments to reporters at the White House on Tuesday, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "make a deal" with Russia and suggested Moscow has the upper hand. Ukraine has been fighting off a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022. In the past, Trump has blamed Zelenskyy for the war and on Tuesday again said it was up to Kyiv to end the Russian invasion. “We want Zelenskyy to make a deal,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. We’ve gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss.” Trump said he also spoke with Putin about Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher detained in Russia accused of acting as a mercenary for Ukrainian forces. "I've been talking to President Putin about Mr. Hubbard. I've been talking to him at length. I've asked him to release him. Let's see what happens," Trump said.
